title: Hi, I’m Manish
text:
I’m a software engineer in Boulder, CO. In my free time I make games in Unity and build little side projects, usually about lakes, water, or making scientific data less annoying to look at.
At my day job at NCAR, I write tools that set up regional ocean simulations in the Community Earth System Model, so scientists spend less time fighting config files. Before that I worked on lake and ice research at the University of Michigan.

🎮 Games: things I’ve made in Unity
🛠️ Projects: personal projects, research code, and work software
✍️ Blog: notes on things that broke and how I fixed them

title: Global Lake Hydrology Explorer
text:
A tool for visualizing lake data worldwide using global precipitation, evaporation, and runoff data. Choose a lake and get a snapshot of its water balance. It’s built to be easy to extend, for watershed modeling or water resource management.
GitHub

title: CrocoDash
text:
CrocoDash is a Python package I develop under the CROCODILE-CESM project at NCAR. It sets up regional MOM6 ocean simulations inside the Community Earth System Model, so researchers can build high-resolution regional configurations without managing the whole model infrastructure by hand.
GitHub Docs DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17342302

title: MonoCopula
text:
The Mono Lake Copula Forecasting Model learns how the parts of the lake’s water balance move together, using vine copulas, then samples thousands of possible futures from that. The correlations are preserved, and the sample size isn’t limited to the historical record.
I wrote up how it works, copulas included, in this blog post.
Docs

title: Apostle Islands Ice Cover Model
text:
A statistical model of coastal ice cover around Lake Superior’s Apostle Islands. It combines satellite ice extent, in situ observations, and climate teleconnections (like ENSO and the Arctic Oscillation) to separate out what drives ice trends and variability.

Venumuddula, M., Kirchner, K., Chen, A., Rood, R. B., & Gronewold, A. D. (2024). Combining satellite, teleconnection, and in situ data to improve understanding of multi-decadal coastal ice cover dynamics on Earth’s largest freshwater lake. Earth and Space Science, 11, e2024EA003845.

Paper (ESS) Code & data

title: Mono Lake Water Balance
text:
A reconstruction of Mono Lake’s water balance that separates human water diversions from climate-driven drought as causes of decades of lake-level decline.

Gossard, A., Venumuddula, M., VanDeWeghe, A., Wegener, C., & Gronewold, A. D. (2025). Differentiating diversions and drought to understand drivers of water loss from a North American terminal lake. Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management.

Paper (JWRPM)

title: visualCaseGen
text:
visualCaseGen gives CESM users an interactive, constraint-solver-assisted way to configure experiments. It encodes the model’s configuration rules as SMT constraints, so invalid setups get caught before they run.

Altuntas, A., Simpson, I. R., Bachman, S. D., Venumuddula, M., Levis, S., Dobbins, B., Sacks, W. J., & Danabasoglu, G. (2026). visualCaseGen: An SMT-based experiment configurator for Community Earth System Model. Journal of Open Source Software.

title: Deploying a Django website as a confused Earth science programmer
text:
Deploying a Django website is hard, especially if you don’t know anything about linux, web servers, or front-end/back-end. In my case of setting up a website for a lake research project, it was impossible. Thankfully, leveraging a couple of very cool tutorials and taking shameless advantage of AWS free tier (which can then be transitioned to a free/cheap non-profit account cuz research is non-profit), we can deploy a Django website in HTTP! HTTPS - which has an extra S - has security, so you need to buy a domain (not free!) and get a free security certificate from something like Let’s Encrypt - a company!
Here is an option to get the deployment working: Steps of Django Deployment on AWS.
I’d only use this tutorial if you’re a python coder who figured out Django, but knows nothing about how webservers (Apache2, NGINX) and linux servers work, which is like very common in earth science.
Feel free to email me when things don’t work, it’s fun to figure out.
